channel.title: The Principles of Board Training
channel.description: Practical California board training for directors preparing for meetings, budgets, audits, executive oversight, minutes, risk, and legal escalation.

item.title: The Board Is Supreme. You Are Not.
item.description: Individual directors have duties and voice, but board authority belongs to the board acting through proper process.

item.title: The Budget Is the Board's Permission Slip
item.description: A budget is not just a spreadsheet; it is the board's authorization for management to spend within a plan.

item.title: Minutes Are Evidence, Not Storytelling
item.description: Good minutes prove what the board did; they do not preserve every comment or smooth over weak process.

item.title: Safety Is a Board Issue
item.description: The board does not run daily safety operations, but it must make sure serious risk is visible, assigned, insured, and reviewed.

item.title: Stop Using Board Meetings to Listen to Reports
item.description: A board agenda should be built around decisions, risks, and judgment, not passive report consumption.

item.title: Trust the Executive Director. Verify the System.
item.description: Healthy oversight is not distrust; it is how the board confirms that authority, reporting, controls, and risk are working.

item.title: Your Board Is Not a Startup Board Anymore
item.description: A working board has to move from founder energy to repeatable oversight, records, controls, and decision discipline.

item.title: The Board Has Not Reviewed Insurance in Years
item.description: A director asks about insurance after a program expansion and no one knows the coverage, exclusions, or renewal process.

item.title: The Board Packet Arrived Too Late
item.description: Directors receive a major decision packet the night before the meeting and are asked to approve anyway.

item.title: A Director Keeps Contacting Staff
item.description: A well-intentioned director bypasses the executive director and gives staff direct requests and instructions.

item.title: The Executive Director Wants a Raise
item.description: A respected executive director requests a compensation increase and directors want to avoid an awkward conversation.

item.title: The Finance Committee Says Everything Is Fine
item.description: The finance committee gives a confident oral update, but the board packet contains thin financial detail.

item.title: The Minutes Are Long, But No One Knows What Passed
item.description: Draft minutes contain pages of discussion but do not clearly show motions, votes, recusals, or assigned follow-up.
